narrative:
The model estimated a 91.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and your law school application was denied on that basis. This is a high estimated risk, not a judgment that failure is certain, but it was strong enough to drive an adverse admissions decision.

The decision was influenced most by your academic standing during law school. Your third-year class-rank decile was the single strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure; being in the first decile is far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students. Your first-year decile was the second most important factor and also pushed toward failure, again at the first decile versus an accepted-student average near 6.00. These two indicators told the model that your grades placed you at the bottom of your class in both early and later years, which is the main reason the predicted bar-failure risk rose so high. Your entrance exam score was the third most important factor, but it pushed slightly toward passing: a score of 37 is essentially at the accepted average of about 37.18, so it did not explain the denial.

Next, ask admissions for a review, explain any circumstances behind your class ranking, and present evidence of academic improvement or a concrete bar-preparation and study-support plan. Strengthening your academic record and demonstrating readiness for bar-level work will matter more than retaking the entrance exam.
